**You Are Home. Your Attention Is Still at Work.**

The plates are on the table when the first message arrives. Someone needs an approval. Someone cannot find the file. A small decision has become urgent because the person who usually makes it is you.

You tell the people beside you that you will be one minute. Then another message opens. When you look up, the conversation has moved somewhere you cannot quite follow, and you nod because explaining that you missed it would make the moment heavier.

The trouble is not that you do not care about being there. You care enough to feel the distance while you are sitting in the same room. A business you built for greater freedom keeps reaching into the hours that were supposed to belong to your life.

**Give the Next Routine Question an Answer That Does Not Have to Be You.**

In Own Your Week, you begin with a bottleneck audit: the work and decisions that keep finding their way back to the owner. Choose an interruption you recognize, and look at what keeps making it yours.

Then the decision-rule worksheet helps you put a boundary around it. What can your team decide? What needs your judgment? What information lets someone move without sending you another message?

Those questions give responsibility a place to go. Picture a team member checking a clear rule and taking the next step while you stay with the conversation in front of you. You have begun changing the arrangement, not merely promising yourself you will ignore the phone.

Give the hours outside work something stronger than another promise to switch off.

**You Handed It Off. Somehow, It Came Back as Your Job.**

You explain the task between meetings, send a few notes, and feel a brief pocket of relief. One thing is finally moving without you having to do every part yourself.

Then the questions arrive. The result is not what you pictured. A detail that felt obvious to you never made it into the instructions. With the deadline getting close, you open the file and finish it yourself because explaining the correction seems slower than making it.

By the end of the day, you have done your work and the work you thought you had delegated. The frustrating part is how familiar the conclusion feels: it is easier to do it myself. Each time you reach it, the business becomes a little more dependent on you.

**Make the Handoff Clear Before the Deadline Makes It Urgent.**

In the owner lab, you work with a handoff template that names the result, the person responsible, and the next step. Instead of assuming someone can see the finished work in your head, you make the expectations visible.

You also connect the handoff to the decisions that person can make and the questions that should come back to you. It becomes easier to see whether a task was actually transferred or merely described in a hurry.

You begin with one task that has come back too many times. By putting its expectations on the page, you give the next conversation something clear to stand on. Picture handing over more than a hurried explanation: a result somebody else can recognize, decisions they can own, and responsibility that no longer lives only in your head.

**There Is Always Time for the Emergency. Your Future Keeps Waiting.**

You open next week's calendar on Sunday evening. The meetings are there. The client deadlines are there. So are the small promises you made while trying to keep everything moving.

The time to think about how the business should work is missing again. There is a process you want to improve and a decision that could make the next month easier, but neither has someone waiting at your door demanding an answer.

So they remain important things you will do when the urgent work clears. The business gets your response all day and your leadership only when there is something left. You can feel how much effort is going into keeping it alive, and how little space remains for choosing what you want it to become.

### 5A: Recognition and reason

That is the reason why I created Own Your Week: the business you built should have room for the life you built it for.

You did not take on this responsibility because your greatest ambition was to answer every question. You had a vision. Work you were proud of. People you wanted to provide for and actually be present with. Somewhere between becoming the owner and becoming everybody's answer, those reasons started waiting. I created this lab because keeping a business alive should not require putting the person who built it on hold.

### 5B: Commitment made concrete

We put the work back where it belongs. We look at the questions that keep returning to you, make responsibility clear, and give leadership a place in your week. These are the decisions underneath the freedom you are trying to build.

This is why the lab works with your actual bottleneck and handoff instead of leaving you with another speech about balance. I want you to see where your attention is going, what you can change, and how to begin. Your vision needs more than your last exhausted hour. It needs a way to become part of the working day.

### 5C: The personal invitation

Think about closing your laptop because the day has a stopping place. Hearing the whole story at dinner. Coming back to work with time to make a decision about where the business goes next. Those moments belong in the reason you are doing this.

Bring that reason into Own Your Week. Bring the work that keeps finding its way back to you. We will put it on the table and begin building a different arrangement. You have already invested so much in becoming the owner. Now make room to live like your time belongs to you, too.

Put the freedom you started this business for back into the decisions you make next.

Own Your Week is for service-business owners who want clearer ways to lead the work, not simply a higher tolerance for interruption. It is designed to serve:

- **The owner whose team waits for routine answers.** You are tired of being needed in every small decision and want clearer boundaries around what comes back to you.
- **The founder who wants room to build.** You want time to think about the next stage of the business before another urgent request fills the opening.
- **The team leader worn down by rework.** You keep finishing tasks you believed you had handed off and want a shared picture of what a good result means.
- **The experienced operator ready to work more deliberately.** The business is moving; you want the structure of your week to reflect where your judgment is genuinely needed.

**Put Structure Behind the Freedom You Started This Business to Create.**

A clearer working week begins with understanding what keeps creating the current one. Own Your Week is a live two-hour owner lab built around six practical inclusions:

- **Find What Keeps Pulling You Back - a bottleneck audit.** Identify work or decisions that repeatedly return to you. You will have a specific pattern to examine instead of labeling the whole business chaotic and trying to repair everything at once.
- **Give Decisions a Clear Owner - a decision-rule worksheet.** Clarify which choices someone else can make and which need your judgment. The worksheet turns a vague request for initiative into boundaries that can be discussed and refined.
- **Hand Over More Than a Task - a handoff template.** Define the desired result, the person responsible, and the next step. Use it to make expectations visible before different assumptions become another urgent correction you handle yourself.
- **Give Your Vision Time - a guided weekly operating-plan exercise.** Look at leadership priorities alongside current commitments. Begin identifying where a piece of strategic work can fit and what needs to support that time.
- **Bring Your Real Questions - live Q&A.** Ask about the tools and the working situations they surface. Use this group discussion to connect the exercises to a working decision you need to make.
- **Keep the Work in Your Hands - an emailed workbook bonus.** Keep the exercises together as a reference for continuing the work with your actual tasks, team conversations, and calendar after the session ends.

Bring the business you built for freedom. Leave with tools you have begun putting behind that freedom.

**[CTA BUTTON: Give My Business Room to Grow]**

Here is how to join Own Your Week and arrive ready to work on something specific, rather than adding another unfinished course to your list.

1. Open the registration form. Enter your details and submit the form. Look for the on-screen confirmation before leaving the page so you know your registration was received.
2. Enter the optional owner community. The link arrives with your confirmation. Use the space to introduce yourself and the kind of business you lead, without posting confidential client information.
3. Save the emailed workbook bonus. Keep the audit, decision-rule, handoff, and planning exercises together so you can use them during the live owner lab.
4. Look for Marcus's welcome text only after choosing SMS updates. The message goes to the number you provide; your email holds the event information and access details.
5. Add the live lab to your calendar. Check the confirmed start time and time zone. Save the access link and bring a recurring bottleneck you can describe without exposing private information.
6. Share the registration link with a fellow owner. Let them decide whether the lab fits their needs and register separately rather than forwarding private access details.
7. Bring the business you built for freedom. Open the workbook beside your calendar, and come ready to give your leadership and your life a place in the week ahead.

You know how to join. Bring the reason you started this business into the work of leading it.

### Part 1: The Big Bold Heartfelt Message

Before you join me, I want you to know why this work reaches beyond a calendar for me. I remember what it felt like to build a business I was proud of and disappear inside it.

### Part 2: The Big Struggle

One evening I sat down to dinner with my phone beside my plate. A routine question came in. I answered it because that seemed easier than leaving someone waiting. Then I checked the next message.

Across the table, people were talking. I nodded in the right places. I even laughed. Then someone asked what I thought, and I had no idea what they were talking about.

I could have blamed a busy day. What I did not want to admit was that being indispensable had become part of how I knew I mattered. Every question wore me out and reassured me at the same time. The business needed me. That felt important, even as the people beside me kept receiving the part of me that was left.

I remember looking at the phone and realizing I had been calling this providing for my family. That was true. It was not the whole truth. I was there, and I was missing them.

### Part 3: The Big Decision

I decided I wanted a business I could lead, not one I had to hold together with my permanent availability. I began writing down the decisions that kept coming back and what somebody else would need to own them.

That changed the work I did. Instead of taking every task back, I began making the expectations clearer. Instead of treating the next message as a measure of my worth, I began asking whether it actually needed me. I was learning to be the owner in a different way.

### Part 4: The Big Reason

Own Your Week grew out of that decision. I wanted a place where owners could look at the patterns they were tired of living inside and do something with what they saw.

The audit, the decision rules, the handoff, and the operating plan belong together because your business and your life do. I care about the responsibility you carry. I also care about what happens when you get home. The freedom you set out to build should have room for both.

### Part 5: The Big Invite

Join me in the live Own Your Week lab. Bring the decision that keeps reaching you after you thought the day was finished. Bring the task you are tired of taking back.

We will work with something you recognize and begin giving the responsibility a clearer home. Your company does not have to be perfectly organized for you to choose a different way of leading it.

### Part 6: The Big Passionate Close

Reserve your place. Put the reason you started this business back into the way you run it.

There is a conversation you deserve to hear from beginning to end. There is a vision that deserves more than your last tired hour. You built the business. Now make room for the life you built it for.

With respect, Marcus Reed
